relationships.name: The neutron spectrometer finds the ice, the drill confirms it
relationships.notice: The drill tests only the ground under it: it cannot tell where the ice is. A neutron spectrometer senses buried hydrogen as the rover drives, so it shows where to drill.
relationships.reviewText: Needs: the drill confirms ice but cannot find it. The neutron spectrometer senses buried hydrogen while the rover drives. Bring the neutron spectrometer to locate the ice and the drill to confirm it; on a tight budget, choose one, or earn points elsewhere.
relationships.reviewSolved: Solved: the neutron spectrometer shows where hydrogen is buried, and the drill confirms the ice.
relationships.debrief: The drill only tests the ground it stands on, so in the dark crater it could not tell how close the ice was. A neutron spectrometer senses hydrogen under the surface as the rover drives, which shows where to dig.
answers: Bring the neutron spectrometer to locate the ice and the drill to confirm it.
On a tight budget, choose one of the two, or earn points with other instruments.
relationships.fact: NASA's VIPER rover is designed to sense hidden water up to about 1 m (3 feet) below the surface with its Neutron Spectrometer System while it drives. VIPER has not flown yet.
relationships.source: NASA Science, VIPER rover and instruments (science.nasa.gov/mission/viper/rover-and-instruments)

relationships.name: The seismometer needs quiet ground
relationships.notice: Moonquake record noisy: the rover drove {closest} m from the station while it listened. The rover's own driving shakes the ground: before the quake, keep at least {distance} m away, or park.
relationships.reviewText: Conditions: the rover's own driving shakes the ground near a deployed seismometer and adds noise. Deploy the station, then drive away before the moonquake, or place it off the return route.
relationships.debrief: The rover's own driving shook the ground near the station, and the seismometer recorded that shaking on top of the moonquake. The record is clean only if the rover is far away, or parked, while the station listens before the quake.
answers: Set the station down early, then drive away.
Set it down where the route does not come back.
Near the station, stop instead of driving: a parked rover is quiet.
relationships.fact: Chandrayaan-3's ILSA seismometer recorded vibrations from its rover's movements on August 25, 2023.
relationships.source: ISRO, ILSA listens to the movements around the landing site (isro.gov.in/Ch3_ILSA_Listens_Landing_Site.html)

relationships.name: In the cold, instruments need the heater
relationships.notice: The cold is slowing the instrument: without a heater, instruments work slowly in permanent shadow.
relationships.reviewText: Needs: in permanent shadow, instruments that hold still work slowly without a heater. Bring a heater, or keep instrument work in sunlight.
relationships.reviewSolved: Solved: the heater keeps instruments working at full speed in permanent shadow.
relationships.debrief: Permanent shadow stays very cold, and the instrument slowed as it chilled. A heater keeps instruments warm enough to work at full speed.
answers: Fit a heater to work in permanent shadow.
Keep instrument work in sunlight.
relationships.fact: NASA's LRO Diviner instrument found that permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles can get as cold as -414 °F (about -248 °C, or 25 K).
relationships.source: NASA SVS 11230, Diviner temperatures of the lunar poles (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11230): shadowed regions as cold as -414 °F

relationships.name: A colder X-ray detector gives sharper readings
relationships.notice: X-ray reading sharper and faster here: the shade keeps the detector cold. In sunlight the reading takes longer.
relationships.reviewText: Conditions: the X-ray spectrometer's detector gives sharper readings when it is colder, so readings in shade finish sooner. Read in shade where you can, or accept slower readings in sunlight.
relationships.debrief: A colder X-ray detector picks out each element's X-rays more sharply, so a clear reading takes less time. The rover was in shade, where the detector stays colder, so the reading finished sooner.
answers: Take readings in shade when the route allows.
Accept slower readings in sunlight.
relationships.fact: Curiosity's X-ray tool gets sharper readings when its detector is colder, so it can switch on a small cooler to chill the detector.
relationships.source: Mars Science Laboratory APXS documentation, Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (an.rsl.wustl.edu/help/Content/About%20the%20mission/MSL/Instruments/APXS%20Alpha%20Particle%20X-ray%20Spectrometer.htm): best resolution below about -15 °C

relationships.name: No lights, no permanent shadow
relationships.notice: Permanent shadow ahead: without lights the rover cannot see the ground, so it stops at the edge. Floodlights would let it drive into the dark.
relationships.reviewText: Without lights, the rover cannot drive into permanent shadow.
relationships.debrief: Permanent shadow never gets sunlight, so a rover without lights cannot see where it is going and has to stop at the edge. Lights let the rover see the ground in the dark.
answers: Fit floodlights.
Plan the mission on sunlit ground, away from the dark crater.
relationships.fact: NASA's VIPER rover was designed to explore dark craters where the Sun never reaches, and it was designed with headlights, a first for a NASA rover. VIPER has not flown yet.
relationships.source: NASA Science, VIPER rover and instruments (science.nasa.gov/mission/viper/rover-and-instruments)

relationships.name: The RTG adds noise to the neutron spectrometer
relationships.notice: The hydrogen meter is noisy: the RTG gives off neutrons of its own, so the meter reads higher than the ground and jitters. A faint rise toward hydrated ground is hard to follow on this rover.
relationships.reviewText: Conflicts: the RTG gives off neutrons of its own, which raise the neutron spectrometer's reading and make it jitter, so faint hydrogen is hard to follow. Use solar power with the neutron spectrometer, or leave the neutron spectrometer home.
relationships.reviewSolved: Solved: on solar power, the neutron spectrometer reads the ground without the RTG's neutrons.
relationships.debrief: An RTG makes power from decaying plutonium, and it also gives off neutrons. The neutron spectrometer counted them on top of the neutrons coming up from the ground, so its reading sat higher and wobbled, hiding the small rise near hydrated ground.
answers: Power the rover with solar panels when it carries the neutron spectrometer.
Leave the neutron spectrometer home on an RTG rover.
relationships.fact: Jun et al. (2013) estimated that about 60% of the thermal neutrons counted by DAN, the neutron instrument on NASA's Curiosity rover, at the Rocknest site came from the rover's own nuclear generator (its MMRTG), and about 40% from cosmic rays.
relationships.source: Jun et al. (2013), Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets 118:2400, doi:10.1002/2013JE004510

relationships.name: Dust on the panels
relationships.notice: Dust has settled on the solar panels and cut their income by {loss}%. It keeps settling every sol, so later sols bring less energy. A dust devil passing close can blow the panels clean.
relationships.reviewText: Conditions: dust settles on solar panels every sol, so solar income falls as the mission goes on. Plan for less power late in the mission. An RTG needs no panels; the vertical solar mast stands higher, where less dust settles; a dust devil passing close blows the panels clean.
relationships.reviewSolved: Solved: the RTG makes its power without panels, so dust cannot dim it.
relationships.debrief: Dust from the air settles on solar panels a little every sol and blocks some of the sunlight, so the panels made less energy as the mission went on. Wind can blow it off: a dust devil that passes close to the rover cleans the panels.
answers: Fit an RTG: its power does not come from panels.
Fit the vertical solar mast: it stands higher, where less dust settles.
Drive past dust devils: one that passes close blows the panels clean.
relationships.fact: In March 2005 the solar power of NASA's Spirit rover jumped sharply in a single sol, as dust on its panels decreased. Dust devils were seen near the rover the next sol, and the team wondered whether one had passed over Spirit and lifted dust off its panels.
relationships.source: Spaceflight Now, Spirit and a dust devil, March 2005 (spaceflightnow.com/mars/mera/050314dustdevil.html)

relationships.name: The organics reading needs gentle ground
relationships.notice: The organics spectrometer rides on the arm, which must hold it right against the rock for the whole long reading. With the rover tilted on steep ground, the arm cannot place it, so the reading is refused. Park on gentler ground near the rock: the arm reaches a few meters.
relationships.reviewText: Conditions: the arm holds the organics spectrometer against a rock only when the rover stands on gentle ground; on a steep slope the reading is refused. Park on level ground beside the target, or on level ground within the arm's reach of it.
relationships.debrief: The organics spectrometer rides on the arm and must sit right against the rock. With the rover tilted on steep ground, the arm could not place it, so the reading was refused. On gentler ground beside the same rock, or within the arm's reach of it, the reading works.
answers: Park on level ground beside the target before reading it.
Use the arm's reach: park on level ground a few meters from a rock on a slope and read it from there.
relationships.fact: NASA's Perseverance rover carries its PIXL and SHERLOC instruments on the turret at the end of its robotic arm. PIXL is placed close to its target rock only after the team judges the placement safe.

relationships.name: No lights, no driving at night
relationships.notice: Night: without lights the rover cannot see the ground, so it cannot drive until dawn. Lights would let it keep driving; without them, power down and sleep through the night.
relationships.reviewText: Without lights, the rover cannot drive at night.
relationships.debrief: At night a rover without lights cannot see where it is going, so it had to stop until dawn. Lights let the rover see the ground in the dark, at a cost in battery.
answers: Fit lights to keep driving at night.
Sleep through the night: power down at sunset and drive again at dawn.
relationships.fact: NASA's Curiosity rover ends its day's work with a nap to recharge its batteries. NASA's VIPER, a Moon rover designed to explore dark craters, was designed with headlights, a first for a NASA rover. VIPER has not flown yet.
relationships.source: JPL, Marking 13 years on Mars, NASA's Curiosity picks up new skills (jpl.nasa.gov/news/marking-13-years-on-mars-nasas-curiosity-picks-up-new-skills); NASA Science, VIPER rover and instruments (science.nasa.gov/mission/viper/rover-and-instruments)
